native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: Higher present-oriented financial behaviour is associated with higher adiposity in NLSY79, but the association is mostly concurrent rather than prospective: measured as a savings-based present-orientation proxy (1989 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview', ordered put-more-in < no-change < took-more-out < no-savings, plus the dis-save/no-savings binary and a net-saving-to-income ratio), it predicts BMI1989 monotonically (mean BMI 24.54 / 24.97 / 25.14 / 25.50; obesity 10.1% / 11.6% / 13.0% / 15.6%; fully adjusted +0.23 BMI units per step, p=0.0002; +0.44 for dis-save-or-no-savings, about 0.1 SD or 1.3 kg), yet holding 1981 body mass fixed removes 54-58% of that gradient (+0.10 per step, p=0.02) and the genuinely prospective 1992 outcome conditional on 1989 BMI is only marginal (+0.06 per step, p=0.08, n=3,861, attrition-fragile and shifted toward the non-black/non-Hispanic cohort). Because higher BMI in 1981 itself predicts more present-oriented saving behaviour in 1989 (+0.013 per BMI unit, p=0.003), the evidence is consistent with a reciprocal wealth/weight/preference process and supports an ASSOCIATION between savings-based present orientation and higher BMI - strongest in women and in the 'no savings' stratum - rather than a demonstrated causal effect of increased time preference on BMI.
